title: Wooden posts and split boards survive 10,500 years beneath a German lake
dek: Divers recovered worked timbers from 20 metres down in Lake Arendsee. The pieces show felling marks and could rewrite what we know about hunter-gatherer building.
body: Archaeologists exploring Lake Arendsee in northern Germany have pulled worked wood from 20 metres underwater that dates to roughly 10,500 years ago. The State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology of Saxony-Anhalt announced the finds after spring 2026 investigations. Among the pieces is a post about 1.6 metres tall bearing clear felling marks and split boards up to 1.3 metres long. Wood from the Mesolithic almost never survives on land, so these timbers offer a rare direct look at how hunter-gatherers shaped their world.

The lake sits in the Altmarkkreis Salzwedel district atop a salt dome that has caused the bottom to subside slowly over millennia. Unlike most inland lakes that fill with sediment and shift their shores, Arendsee has preserved parts of its ancient shoreline beneath a thin sediment layer. That geological quirk kept the wood waterlogged and oxygen-poor, the conditions that stop decay. Researchers had already known people lived along these shores during the Middle Stone Age. The Shaman of Bad Dürrenberg, a celebrated Mesolithic burial, comes from the same region.

State archaeologist Harald Meller said the wood sheds completely new light on a period known in Central Germany mostly from soil discolourations where posts once stood. Project manager Marcel Weiß stressed that whether the timbers formed huts or some other construction remains the subject of ongoing research. If they turn out to be permanent structures or intensively used living areas, they would predate the first farming longhouses in Central Europe by about 3,000 years. That would force a rethink of how mobile or settled Mesolithic communities really were.

After the initial discovery, a second survey brought in the Fraunhofer IOSB-AST in Ilmenau. A remotely operated vehicle equipped with high-resolution sonar mapped the submerged landscape and traced the contours of the former shoreline. By pinning the exact position of each find, the team hopes to spot concentrations that mark archaeological sites and guide future dives. Diving operations manager Sven Thomas called the technology invaluable for underwater archaeology.

Lake Arendsee has already yielded Neolithic fish weirs, a High Medieval flat-bottomed cargo vessel and a Late Medieval dugout canoe. The new finds push the lake's archaeological record much further back and could provide unusually direct evidence of Mesolithic woodworking. Researchers are now trying to determine whether the posts and boards formed huts, another known structure type or something not yet identified in the record. The answer could give a rare glimpse of buildings that survived underwater while nearly all comparable traces on land vanished.
doesnt_show: The finds do not yet show what kind of structure the timbers formed, whether the site was occupied year-round or seasonally, or how widespread such building was among Mesolithic groups.
settle: Detailed spatial analysis of the timber positions combined with further radiocarbon dates and microwear studies on the wood surfaces would clarify the structure type and intensity of use.
